DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The proposal's central claims don't hold up. The revenue figure uses the wrong room count. The price-sensitivity "test" is confounded by seasonality. The two-night minimum conflicts with the hotel's largest Saturday segment. The £204,000 is not a floor; it is an overstatement with unquantified downside risk.

## 1. The revenue calculation uses the wrong room count

Section 2 says Harbourside has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124 rooms**.

- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£203,800**, which is where the £204,000 comes from.
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**.

The headline figure is about £20,000 (11%) too high before any other adjustment. The recommendation repeats it as "at least £204,000".

## 2. The figure assumes every occupied room pays BAR

The £20 uplift is applied to all occupied weekend rooms. But the proposal says corporate and contracted group rates are unchanged, and wedding blocks are ~38% of Saturday bookings. Those rooms won't see the £20 rise, nor will rooms on packages or other negotiated rates. OTA commission also reduces net gain on bookings through those channels. The real uplift depends on the BAR-paying share of weekend rooms, which isn't given. It is likely well below even the corrected £184,000.

## 3. The price-sensitivity "test" doesn't test price sensitivity

The rate rose in the last week of June 2025, and July occupancy rose from 81% to 89%. But the document itself explains July: the **harbour festival and school summer holidays** make July and August the peak months. Any June-to-July comparison would show a rise regardless of price.

- There is no control: no comparison with July 2024, with competitors' July movement, or with demand forecasts.
- June 2025 (81%) was itself below May (85%), so the baseline is a dip month.
- One month of data, at a +£10 change, can't support conclusions about a +£20 change at a higher price point.

The conclusion that "our weekend guests are not price sensitive", and the claim that the rise "reinforced our positioning", aren't supported. The proposal's assumption that occupancy holds rests entirely on this.

## 4. The value-for-money score cuts the other way

A score of 8.4 was earned at £135–£145, *below* the comp set. It shows guests think they're getting a good deal at a low price. That is partly *because* of the low price. It isn't evidence they'll accept £165, and the score would likely fall as the gap to competitors closes. At £165 the hotel sits at the bottom of the comp set's range (£165–£180), not below it. Its price advantage disappears.

## 5. The two-night minimum conflicts with the wedding business

Section 4 states that ~38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests who arrive Saturday and leave Sunday, i.e. single-night stays. A two-night minimum on any stay including Saturday would either:

- force these guests to pay for an unwanted Friday night, or
- push them to competitors.

The proposal only protects group rates *already contracted*. Future wedding blocks, and wedding guests booking individually, are exposed. This segment fills the hotel's most constrained night, yet the proposal treats the minimum purely as upside. It says the extra nights are "material" but unquantified, and assigns no value to the risk of losing over a third of Saturday demand. It also offers no evidence that other single-night Saturday guests will extend rather than book elsewhere.

## 6. "Conservative" and "floor" are not justified

The estimate excludes the minimum-stay *upside* but also ignores its *downside*. It assumes occupancy is unchanged despite a 14% rate rise and a new booking restriction. Combined with points 1–2, £204,000 is better described as an upper-bound scenario than a floor.

## 7. The monitoring trigger is weak and slow

- The trigger is a full month of actuals falling **more than five points** below 2025. At that point bookings for following weeks are already priced, and five points is significant lost revenue. On corrected figures, roughly 112 rooms × ~9 weekend nights × 5% × £165 is about £8,000+ per month in room revenue alone, before ancillary spend.
- The response is only to "review the rate". There is no defined rollback, and no separate trigger for the minimum-stay rule, so the two effects can't be told apart.
- Weekly pick-up tracking is useful but has no thresholds attached.
- The 2025 baseline months are themselves noisy (see June), making the comparison unreliable.

## 8. Smaller points

- Two weeks' OTA notice (15 May for 1 June) is short. It doesn't address bookings already held for June at the old rate or rate-parity implications.
- Applying the rise to Friday as well as Saturday isn't separately justified. Saturday is the constrained night (31 sell-outs), but Friday demand may be softer.
- Introducing both changes on the same date makes it impossible to attribute any occupancy change to one or the other.

## Recommendations

1. Correct the room count to 112 and recalculate on BAR-paying rooms only, net of commission.
2. Replace the June/July comparison with a year-on-year or comp-set-adjusted analysis. Without one, state openly that price sensitivity is unknown.
3. Model a downside scenario for occupancy, e.g. −3 and −6 points.
4. Exempt wedding guests (e.g. via a group/promo code) or drop the minimum on wedding Saturdays, and quantify the minimum-stay effect both ways.
5. Consider phasing: Saturday-only rate rise first, or a trial on non-peak months, with the minimum introduced separately.
6. Tighten monitoring with weekly pick-up thresholds, a lower trigger, and a pre-agreed rollback action.

As written, the proposal shouldn't be approved on the basis that it is "well-evidenced" and "low-risk". A rate increase may well be justified given the comp-set gap, but the evidence and revenue case need rebuilding first.
